one_liner: rustc's own tiny multiply-based hasher and FxHashMap/FxHashSet aliases. Much faster than std SipHash-1-3 on integer-heavy keys, but not DoS-resistant.
what_it_does: Provides FxHasher, a non-cryptographic Hasher built for the small integer, pointer and tuple keys that dominate rustc's hash tables. It also provides FxHashMap/FxHashSet, which are plain type aliases for std's HashMap/HashSet with the zero-sized FxBuildHasher, so the whole std API is kept. There are opt-in variants: FxSeededState (fixed seed) and, behind the `rand` feature, FxRandomState and FxHashMapRand/FxHashSetRand (random seed per map). The crate is no_std-capable with default features off.
how_it_is_fast: Each integer write is one add and one multiply, `hash = (hash + x) * K`, with K a Steele–Vigna MCG multiplier. This makes a polynomial hash over the Hasher's write calls. finish() is a single rotate_left(26) (15 on 32-bit), which moves the well-mixed high bits of the product into the low bits hashbrown uses as its bucket index. Byte strings and slices are first compressed to one u64 by a small wyhash-style routine: 16-byte chunks go through a 64x64->128 folded multiply (lo ^ hi) in two independent lanes. There is no per-map state and all functions are small #[inline] code. A single-integer key costs roughly one multiply plus a rotate, against SipHash-1-3's multi-word state setup and rounds.
when_to_use: Hash maps/sets in compilers, analyzers, graph code or ECS-style code keyed by integers, IDs, pointers/interned handles or small tuples of them, where profiling shows hashing is hot.
Internal tables whose keys are never controlled by an attacker (build tools, offline batch jobs, single-user CLIs).
When you want deterministic iteration order within one build and platform and no per-map seed (FxBuildHasher is zero-sized, so the map carries no hasher state).
no_std or embedded targets that need a tiny dependency-free Hasher (disable default features).
Workloads shaped like rustc's own. In rustc profiling cited in PR #37, the four most common hash-call shapes, each 1-3 integer writes, made up about 74% of calls.
when_not_to_use: Any map keyed by untrusted input (network, user-supplied strings). It has no HashDoS resistance, and the hash is linear, so colliding keys are easy to construct, even by accident.

Building one large map by inserting keys in another Fx map's iteration order, as in serde/bincode deserialization or cloning via iteration. Issue #45 (open since 2.0; a 2026 comment says it still bites) reports about 8-9x slowdowns at 10M u64 keys, and random seeding does not help because the hash is linear in the seed.

Very large tables of low-entropy keys such as aligned pointers. The fixed rotate only spreads entropy well up to about 2^26 buckets. In 2.0 the rotate of 20 caused a roughly 3x rustc compile-time blowup on one large project (rust#135477), which 2.1.1 only mitigated.

When you need hash values that are stable across crate versions or targets. 2.x changed the output in minor releases (issue #58), and 32-bit, sparc64 and wasm64 use a different byte-hash path (issue #73).

String-heavy or long-key workloads, where general-purpose hashers are a better fit. Even for integer keys, Nethercote's microbenchmark showed std HashMap (with his unmerged SipHash patch) slightly ahead of the old FxHashMap, because it had fewer collisions.

integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.77 (rust-version in Cargo.toml since 2.1.2), edition 2021; `nightly` feature needs a nightly compiler
integration.platforms: any; fast 64x64->128 multiply path on 64-bit targets such as x86-64 and aarch64; 32-bit decomposed fallback on 32-bit targets, sparc64 and wasm64 without wide-arithmetic. CI covers Linux/macOS/Windows plus Miri on x86_64, i686, mips and mips64 (big-endian).
integration.thread_safety: Same as std HashMap, since the aliases are std types. FxHasher and FxBuildHasher hold only plain integers. FxRandomState draws its seed from a thread-local, then increments it for each new map.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — FxHashMap<K,V> is std HashMap<K,V,FxBuildHasher>, so the full API works. However, HashMap::new()/with_capacity() exist only for RandomState, so you construct with FxHashMap::default() or with_capacity_and_hasher(n, Default::default()). The type is also not interchangeable with HashMap<K,V> in public signatures.

gotchas: The default seed is 0, so hashing 0 gives 0 and leading zero writes vanish: (0u64, x) hashes the same as x alone. The polynomial structure also gives easy wrapping collisions: (a, b) and (a+1, b-K) collide.

The `nightly` feature makes write_length_prefix a no-op for speed. As the source comment says, nested collections of non-byte-slice elements then lose prefix-freeness and can collide when only the split point differs.

The name is historical. 2.x is Orson Peters' polynomial hash, not the Firefox rotate-xor-multiply FxHash, so older quality critiques and benchmarks (aHash's compare page, foldhash's `fxhash` column, which uses the separate fxhash 0.2.1 crate) do not describe it exactly.
The repo has no benchmarks by design: benchmarks PR #50 was closed because rustc-perf is the only yardstick. 1.2.0 was yanked for no_std breakage.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose rustc-hash over foldhash (same designer; per-map random seed, stronger finalizer, geometric mean 6.21 vs SipHash's 28.70 on its Xeon suite) when keys are trusted integers or pointers and you want the fewest instructions per hash, a zero-sized hasher and deterministic output. Choose foldhash or aHash (keyed, AES-accelerated, some DoS resistance) when keys are strings, externally supplied, or bulk-reinserted between maps. xxHash, rapidhash and wyhash are byte-stream hashers rather than Rust Hasher-trait integer mixers, so they are not direct substitutes here.
verified_claims_summary: In Feb 2020 rustc maintainer N. Nethercote rebuilt rustc with every FxHashMap/FxHashSet switched to std's DefaultHasher (SipHash-1-3) and ran rustc-perf locally. Every `check` benchmark regressed by 3.9%-84.7% (per-benchmark averages 5.9%-63.6%). That baseline included his proposed SipHasher integer speedups (rust PR #69152), which were never merged. Against unpatched std he reported check-clean slowdowns of 4.3%-128.6%. Hardware, compiler flags and the rustc-perf metric were not stated. The test used the old Firefox-derived FxHash. The current 2.x algorithm was only shown to be 'slightly better' for rustc (rust-timer perf runs), with no standalone numbers.
status_note: Actively maintained under the rust-lang org (2.1.3 released 2026-07, last commit 2026-07-18). It is dual Apache-2.0/MIT with no unsafe code and no default dependencies, so it is trivial to depend on or vendor. Its design goals are strictly 'whatever makes rustc faster', not general-purpose quality or output stability.
